advances:
A hypothetical counterexample in the accepted residual strip has a three-direction certificate at an actual maximizing middle point: all three cut masses are equal, their middle boundary lines are concurrent, and each cut admits two equal-length outer subchords whose combined first moment balances the full middle chord. This holds for arbitrary convex polygons, including cuts on exposed edges. Compatibility then places the maximizing point in the central fraction \(2-\sqrt3\) of every active middle chord.

This supplies a simultaneous geometric constraint absent from independent cap-area tables. The remaining area implication \(d\ge 2T/9\) for these concurrent equal-mass cuts is open; this candidate proves the reduction and chord inequalities, not that implication.
author: r129-joint-geometry
proof:
First we justify attainment and the active directions. For \(w\in A_1\), a unit vector \(q\), and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), put

\[
G(w,q,\lambda)=\sum_{i=0}^2
\left|A_i\cap\{x:q\cdot(x-w)+\lambda(i-1)\le0\}\right|.
\tag{5}
\]

The exact profile identity in accepted fact `d2d117bcc58a1ba0` gives
\(h_S((1,w))=\min\{\inf_{q,\lambda}G(w,q,\lambda),a_0+a_1,a_1+a_2\}\). Finite slope attainment, needed here in addition to that profile description, follows directly from compactness. Choose a bounded neighborhood \(U\) of \(A_1\), and a number \(B\) strictly larger than every \(\lVert x-w\rVert\) with \(x\in A_0\cup A_1\cup A_2\) and \(w\in U\). For \(\lambda\ge B\), the outer contributions in (5) are exactly \(a_0,0\), respectively; for \(\lambda\le-B\), they are exactly \(0,a_2\). Consequently the infimum equals the minimum over the fixed compact parameter set \(\mathbb S^1\times[-B,B]\), for every \(w\in U\).

The function \(G\) is jointly continuous there. Indeed, convergence of the parameters gives pointwise convergence of each halfplane indicator except on its limiting boundary line, which has planar area zero; dominated convergence applies on each fixed polygon. The minimum of a continuous function over a fixed compact set is continuous, so middle depth is continuous on \(A_1\).

Middle depth is zero on \(\partial A_1\). To see this, let \(w\in\partial A_1\), choose a supporting unit normal \(n\), and put \(b=n\cdot w=\max_{A_1}n\cdot x\). Compatibility implies
\(\max_{A_0}n\cdot x+\max_{A_2}n\cdot x\le2b\). Choose
\(\gamma\in[\max_{A_0}n\cdot x-b,\ b-\max_{A_2}n\cdot x]\). The closed halfspace \(n\cdot(x-w)+\gamma(h-1)\ge0\) contains \((1,w)\), and on each slice it meets the polygon only in a supporting line or the empty set. Its mass is zero. At any interior middle point, a disk contained in \(A_1\) and centered at the point contributes a positive semidisk area to every proper halfspace through the point; horizontal halfspaces have positive mass as well. Thus middle depth is positive somewhere.

It follows that its positive maximum \(d\) is attained at a point \(z\in\operatorname{int}A_1\). The assumed absence of a middle point of depth \(t\), together with attainment, gives \(d<t\). The area hypotheses give \(a_0+a_1,a_1+a_2>T/2>t\), so at \(z\) only proper halfspaces can attain depth. Define the nonempty compact active set
\(\mathcal A=\{(q,\lambda)\in\mathbb S^1\times[-B,B]:G(z,q,\lambda)=d\}\).

The convex hull of its unit normals contains the origin. Otherwise finite-dimensional strict separation supplies a vector \(v\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(q\cdot v>\varepsilon\) for every active normal. By compactness this inequality, with \(\varepsilon/2\), holds on a neighborhood of \(\mathcal A\) in the parameter set. On the compact complement the value of \(G(z,q,\lambda)\) exceeds \(d\) by a uniform positive amount. For small \(u>0\), replacing \(z\) by \(z+uv\) strictly increases every nearby active cap mass: all three thresholds increase by \(u q\cdot v\), and the middle contribution increases by a uniformly positive constant times \(u\). The latter assertion follows by taking a disk of fixed positive radius centered at \(z\) inside \(A_1\); the small strip swept through this disk has uniformly positive chord length in every direction. Uniform continuity preserves the positive gap on the compact complement. The horizontal terms also exceed \(d\). Therefore \(h_S((1,z+uv))>d\) for small \(u>0\), a contradiction.

Planar Caratheodory now selects at most three active normals whose convex hull contains zero. One unit normal cannot suffice. Two would be opposite. For opposite active normals, write the two cuts as
\(q\cdot(x-z)+\lambda(h-1)\le0\) and \(-q\cdot(x-z)+\lambda'(h-1)\le0\). Their middle sections cover the plane. Their height-zero sections cover the plane when \(\lambda+\lambda'\ge0\), and their height-two sections cover the plane when \(\lambda+\lambda'\le0\). Hence their total mass is at least \(a_1+m\), and \(2d\ge a_1+m\).

On the other hand, \(M<T/2\) gives \(M<a_1+m\), so
\(2t=4T/9<8(a_1+m)/9<a_1+m\). This contradicts \(d<t\). A minimal selected family therefore has exactly three normals. Its convex coefficients are positive, and no pair is parallel; otherwise a smaller family or an opposite pair would suffice. This proves all assertions in (1). The strict area inequalities used here hold in accepted fact `15bb2c1680a0254e`; no further property of its residual strip is needed.

We next prove the selected-section balance, retaining supporting-edge cases. Fix one active cut and temporarily suppress its index \(j\). Its unit normal and slope are \(q,\lambda\). With \(z\) fixed, this cut is a global minimum of (5) over all proper halfspaces through \((1,z)\). We may perturb the normal in all of \(\mathbb R^2\), rather than only tangentially to \(\mathbb S^1\), because a nonzero perturbed normal can be divided by its norm, together with the slope, without changing the halfspace.

For a perturbation \((u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R\), use the cuts
\((q+\eta u)\cdot(x-z)+(\lambda+\eta\tau)(i-1)\le0\), with \(\eta\downarrow0\). On a full boundary section \(L_i\), write
\(v_i(x)=(x-z,i-1)\in\mathbb R^3\) and \(\psi_i(x)=u\cdot(x-z)+\tau(i-1)\). The first directional derivative of the slice contribution is

\[
\begin{cases}
-\displaystyle\int_{L_i} \psi_i(x)\,d\mathcal H_1(x),
&\text{if the line meets }\operatorname{int}A_i,\\[3pt]
\displaystyle\int_{L_i}(-\psi_i(x))_+\,d\mathcal H_1(x),
&\text{if the cap is empty and }L_i\text{ is a supporting edge},\\[3pt]
-\displaystyle\int_{L_i}(\psi_i(x))_+\,d\mathcal H_1(x),
&\text{if the cap is full and }L_i\text{ is a supporting edge},\\[3pt]
0,&\text{if }L_i\text{ is empty or a point}.
\end{cases}
\tag{6}
\]

Here an empty or full cap is understood up to its null boundary. For completeness, take signed normal coordinate \(\nu\) with the old cut \(\nu\le0\), and arclength coordinate along its boundary. At a boundary point \(x\), the perturbed threshold in the normal coordinate is
\(-\eta\psi_i(x)/(1+\eta u\cdot q)\). At an interior point of a transverse chord the swept width is this signed quantity; at a supporting edge only the inward or outward positive part contributes. Integrating along the fixed segment gives (6). Changes near the finitely many polygon vertices contribute \(O(\eta^2)\), since their relevant lengths and normal displacements are both \(O(\eta)\). A point section also creates or removes only such wedges. This proves (6), including its one-sided edge formulas.

Define a compact convex set \(Z_i\subset\mathbb R^3\) of possible negative section moments. At a transverse cut let
\(Z_i=\{-\int_{L_i}v_i(x)\,d\mathcal H_1(x)\}\). At an empty or point section let \(Z_i=\{0\}\). At a supporting edge let
\(Z_i=\{-\int_Ev_i(x)\,d\mathcal H_1(x):E\text{ is a subsegment of }L_i\}\), with a zero-length selection included.

We verify the asserted convexity in the supporting-edge case, where it is essential. Parameterize the edge by arclength \(\theta\in[0,L]\). A subsegment of length \(e\) has first arclength moment \(p\) satisfying exactly

\[
0\le e\le L,\qquad
\frac{e^2}{2}\le p\le Le-\frac{e^2}{2}.
\tag{7}
\]

Conversely every pair in (7) is realized by the interval \([p/e-e/2,p/e+e/2]\) when \(e>0\), and by a zero-length selection when \(e=0\). The region (7) is compact and convex: its lower bound is convex in \(e\), and its upper bound is concave. Since \(v_i(x(\theta))\) is affine in \(\theta\), the negative vector integral is a linear function of \((e,p)\). Its image \(Z_i\) is consequently compact and convex.

Let \(Z=Z_0+Z_1+Z_2\). Formula (6) shows that every directional derivative of the total cut mass lies between
\(\min_{\xi\in Z}\xi\cdot(u,\tau)\) and \(\max_{\xi\in Z}\xi\cdot(u,\tau)\). In fact the empty-edge derivative is the maximum over its \(Z_i\), and the full-edge derivative is the minimum: the positive or negative set of the affine function \(\psi_i\) on a segment is itself a subsegment, so the indicated extrema integrate exactly its relevant positive part.

If \(0\notin Z\), strict separation from the compact convex set \(Z\) yields a perturbation \((u,\tau)\) with \(\max_{\xi\in Z}\xi\cdot(u,\tau)<0\). The corresponding directional derivative is negative, contradicting that the active cut minimizes mass through the fixed point. Therefore \(0\in Z\). By the definitions of the summands, there are actual selected subsegments \(E_0,E_2\), with full sections used at transverse cuts, such that
\(\int_{E_0}v_0+\int_{L_1}v_1+\int_{E_2}v_2=0\). The middle section is transverse because \(z\in\operatorname{int}A_1\). The last coordinate of this equality is \(-|E_0|+|E_2|=0\), and its first two coordinates give (2). Thus one common selection supplies both the equal length and the vector first moment; the two conditions were not obtained from separate choices.

Finally suppose \(\ell>0\). The two selected segments are parallel, have equal length \(\ell\), and lie on the respective endpoint boundary lines. Their midpoint sum is therefore a segment of length \(\ell\) centered at \(c=(c_0+c_2)/2\). Compatibility puts this segment in \(A_1\), and averaging the two boundary equations puts it on \(q\cdot(x-z)=0\). Hence it is contained in \(L_1\). Writing \(b=|L_1|\) and \(c_1\) for its midpoint gives
\(\ell\le b\) and \(\lVert c-c_1\rVert\le(b-\ell)/2\). The first moments in (2) equal \(\ell(c_0-z)+b(c_1-z)+\ell(c_2-z)\), proving (4). Rearranging it yields

\[
\lVert z-c_1\rVert
=\frac{2\ell}{b+2\ell}\lVert c-c_1\rVert
\le\frac{\ell(b-\ell)}{b+2\ell}.
\tag{8}
\]

If \(\ell=0\), (2) gives \(c_1=z\), so (8) and \(\ell\le b\) still hold. Put \(x=\ell/b\in[0,1]\). The function \(x(1-x)/(1+2x)\) has derivative \((1-2x-2x^2)/(1+2x)^2\), so its maximum occurs at \(x=(\sqrt3-1)/2\) and equals \(1-\sqrt3/2\). Dividing (8) by \(b\) proves (3).

Accepted fact `d2d117bcc58a1ba0` ensures that a global counterexample has no middle depth point at level \(t\), while accepted fact `15bb2c1680a0254e` supplies the strict area hypotheses. Thus the reduction applies to the canonical residual problem. No lower bound on the common cut mass beyond the displayed necessary conditions has been asserted.
statement:
Let \(A_0,A_1,A_2\subset\mathbb R^2\) be compact two-dimensional convex polygons satisfying \((A_0+A_2)/2\subseteq A_1\). Put \(a_i=|A_i|\), \(T=a_0+a_1+a_2\), \(M=\max\{a_0,a_2\}\), \(m=\min\{a_0,a_2\}\), and \(t=2T/9\). Assume \(a_i<T/2\) for all \(i\), as holds in the residual strip of accepted fact `15bb2c1680a0254e`. Set \(S=\bigcup_{i=0}^2(\{i\}\times A_i)\), let \(\mu\) be the sum of planar area on these three slices, and define \(h_S(y)=\inf\{\mu(H):H\text{ is a closed halfspace containing }y\}\). Assume that no point \((1,w)\), \(w\in A_1\), has depth at least \(t\).

There are a point \(z\in\operatorname{int}A_1\), a number \(0<d<t\), pairwise nonparallel unit vectors \(q_1,q_2,q_3\), real slopes \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3\), and positive numbers \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\) such that:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d&=\max_{w\in A_1}h_S((1,w)),&
\sum_{j=1}^3\alpha_j&=1,&
\sum_{j=1}^3\alpha_jq_j&=0,\\
\widehat H_j&=\{(h,w):q_j\cdot(w-z)+\lambda_j(h-1)\le0\},&
\mu(\widehat H_j)&=d\qquad(j=1,2,3).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]

For every \(j\), define the full planar boundary section
\(L_{ij}=A_i\cap\{w:q_j\cdot(w-z)+\lambda_j(i-1)=0\}\), and write \(b_j=\mathcal H_1(L_{1j})>0\) and \(c_{1j}\) for the midpoint of the segment \(L_{1j}\). There exist selected segments \(E_{0j}\subseteq L_{0j}\) and \(E_{2j}\subseteq L_{2j}\), with the empty set allowed as a zero-length selection, for which

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal H_1(E_{0j})&=\mathcal H_1(E_{2j})=:\ell_j,\\
\int_{E_{0j}}(w-z)\,d\mathcal H_1(w)
+\int_{L_{1j}}(w-z)\,d\mathcal H_1(w)
+\int_{E_{2j}}(w-z)\,d\mathcal H_1(w)&=0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

The selection has the following precise relation to each full outer section. If the boundary line meets \(\operatorname{int}A_i\), then \(E_{ij}=L_{ij}\). If the boundary line is a supporting line with a nondegenerate exposed edge, \(E_{ij}\) may be a subsegment of that edge. If the boundary line misses \(A_i\) or meets it at one point, its selected length is zero. Thus selected lengths are full chord lengths at transverse cuts; the statement does not identify a selected edge length with the length of the full exposed edge.

These objects satisfy the exact geometric inequalities

\[
0\le\ell_j\le b_j,\qquad
\lVert z-c_{1j}\rVert
\le\frac{\ell_j(b_j-\ell_j)}{b_j+2\ell_j}
\le\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)b_j.
\tag{3}
\]

When \(\ell_j>0\), if \(c_{0j},c_{2j}\) are the midpoints of the two selected segments and \(c_j=(c_{0j}+c_{2j})/2\), then

\[
\frac{E_{0j}+E_{2j}}2\subseteq L_{1j},\qquad
b_j(c_{1j}-z)+2\ell_j(c_j-z)=0.
\tag{4}
\]

When \(\ell_j=0\), equation (2) instead says \(c_{1j}=z\), without introducing midpoints of empty selections.

The normalization of (1) is \(g_j(w)=\alpha_jq_j\cdot(w-z)\) and \(\sigma_j=\alpha_j\lambda_j\), so \(\sum_jg_j=0\). These are concurrent cuts at the attained optimum. Accepted fact `d2d117bcc58a1ba0` uses \(\sum_j f_j=-1\) for a strictly shifted covering certificate; its \(f_j\) are not identified with the \(g_j\) here. Every global counterexample covered by the two declared accepted facts satisfies the assumptions of this statement.
